@Tbl-vol3-01_introduction-key-equations summarizes the quantitative relations used throughout this chapter to evaluate reliability and cost across an execution horizon, where $\PerStepErrorRate$ is the per-step error rate, $\TurnHorizon$ is the horizon length in turns, and $\IndependentAttemptCount$ is the allocated retry budget. @Sec-vol3-agent-economics-accounting measures cost per accepted task over a whole cohort of initiated tasks.

| Equation                                                                                      | What it bounds or decides                                                                                                                   | Where derived                      |
|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------|
| $\Pr(\text{success}) = (1-\PerStepErrorRate)^{\TurnHorizon}$                                  | Task success probability when all $\TurnHorizon$ independent steps must succeed without intermediate checks or recovery                     | @eq-vol3-horizon-compounding       |
| $(1-\PerStepErrorRate)^{\TurnHorizon} \approx e^{-\PerStepErrorRate \TurnHorizon}$            | Under the independent-step model without recovery and at small step error, the product $\PerStepErrorRate \TurnHorizon$ governs reliability | @sec-vol3-intro-horizon-arithmetic |
| $\CostPerAcceptedTask = \mathbb{E}[\AttemptCost]/\AcceptanceProbability$                      | Expected cost per accepted task under independent retries; acceptance rate scales effective attempt cost                                    | @eq-vol3-cost-per-accepted-task    |
| $\MechanismAttemptCost/\MechanismAcceptanceProbability < \AttemptCost/\AcceptanceProbability$ | Economic condition determining whether an added check, boundary, cache, or prompt optimization justifies its cost                           | @sec-vol3-intro-horizon-arithmetic |
| $1-(1-\AcceptanceProbability)^{\IndependentAttemptCount}$                                     | Cumulative acceptance probability within a budget of $\IndependentAttemptCount$ attempts, assuming independent failures                     | @sec-vol3-intro-fallacies          |
: **Key Equations of the Introduction**: Each relation prices reliability or operational cost over an execution trajectory; the first two govern unchecked horizons, while the remaining equations determine whether a specific mechanism justifies its cost. {#tbl-vol3-01_introduction-key-equations tbl-colwidths="[46,36,18]"}

::: {.callout-takeaways title="Agency is a property of the system, not the model"}

* **Stochastic proposals need a closing runtime**: An agent resembles a classical computer, but its foundation model only proposes. It generates candidate tokens and actions, leaving the validation of correctness and actual execution to external software. The surrounding runtime must enforce permissions, preserve state across steps, and govern the full trajectory through failures and retries.
* **Task exposure dictates architectural obligations**: The H·S·A dimensions (horizon length, accumulated state, and delegated authority) pinpoint where an autonomous workflow requires protective sandboxes, durable checkpoints, human intervention, and verifiable evidence. System mechanisms should scale with this exposure profile; tasks with short horizons and constrained authority do not require the heavyweight control loops of high-exposure systems.
* **Runtime enforcement and empirical evidence serve distinct roles**: Structural boundaries enforce hard constraints on permitted actions, preventing catastrophic side effects regardless of model behavior. By contrast, verification checks produce empirical evidence only for the specific properties they measure. Task acceptance requires evaluating this evidence against a defined contract. Passing tests support claims only within their measured coverage; an eloquent report alone supplies no independent evidence.
* **Two numbers price every mechanism, autonomy included**: Under the independent-step model without recovery, unchecked task success decays exponentially with horizon length, so detecting and repairing errors before later turns depend on them can improve reliability without changing the model. Meanwhile, the cost per accepted task amortizes all wasted inference, compute infrastructure, and human oversight across verified deliverables. An autonomous loop justifies its operational complexity only when it reduces this net cost under the task contract.

:::

## Historical Perspective and Further Reading {#sec-vol3-intro-history}

The closed-loop architecture at the core of agentic systems predates modern machine learning by decades. In founding cybernetics, Norbert Wiener established feedback as the organizing principle of control: a system observes its environment, measures the discrepancy between current state and a target goal, and applies corrective actions [@wiener1948cybernetics]. Writing a decade later, Wiener warned of the operational hazard inherent in rapid feedback: when an automated machine acts faster than a human operator can intervene, it must be constrained to the exact purpose intended [@wiener1960]. Artificial intelligence adopted this structure through the rational agent framework, defining an agent by its continuous cycle of perception and environment interaction [@russell2020artificial]. Reinforcement learning subsequently formalized that cycle, treating the iterative trajectory of states, actions, rewards, and observations as the central object of learning [@sutton2018reinforcement].

What transformed with foundation models was the capability of the component driving the loop. Rather than relying on specialized heuristics or hand-crafted policies, a general-purpose model pretrained across diverse data distributions can now synthesize reasoning traces and emit concrete actions in text and code [@bommasani2021opportunities]. The ReAct architecture demonstrated that interleaving model-generated reasoning with tool execution feedback allows language models to operate effectively in open software environments [@yao2023react]. Real-world software engineering benchmarks crystallized this shift, demonstrating that an agent's capability must be measured not by fluency on static prompts, but by whether its proposed patches pass unseen repository test suites [@jimenez2024swebench].

The scaffolding surrounding the model builds on classical systems research addressing unreliable components. John von Neumann first investigated how to synthesize dependable computational systems from failure-prone parts, demonstrating that modular redundancy, majority voting, and periodic state restoration can bound compound failure rates [@vonneumann1956probabilistic]. Subsequent distributed systems research formalized the fault assumptions that supervisors must accommodate. These range from fail-stop models, where damaged components halt detectably [@schlichting1983failstop], to Byzantine failure models, where components behave arbitrarily or deceptively [@lamport1982byzantine]. The modern dependability taxonomy codified the causal sequence linking latent faults, runtime errors, and observable system failures, drawing an essential distinction between errors that trigger overt alarms and those that silently corrupt downstream execution [@avizienis2004basic].

Because foundation models generate probabilistic outputs, verification cannot be offloaded to the generator itself. The end-to-end argument in system design established that complete correctness checks cannot be delegated to intermediate subcomponents; they must ultimately reside at the endpoint that understands application-level task requirements [@saltzer1984endtoend]. At the same time, Dijkstra's foundational observation that software testing demonstrates the presence of bugs rather than their absence bounds the certainty that any validation suite can provide [@dijkstra1970structured].

Managing delegation and authority safely relies on principles developed across operating systems and distributed transaction design. Capability-based addressing, introduced by Dennis and Van Horn, bound access rights directly to unforgeable, fine-grained object references rather than ambient process identities [@dennis1966]. Saltzer and Schroeder codified these patterns into enduring design principles for computer protection, emphasizing least privilege, complete mediation of access requests, and economy of mechanism [@saltzer1975]. Hardy later uncovered the hazard of ambient authority: in a confused deputy attack, an unprivileged client manipulates a privileged utility into misusing permissions granted by its environment rather than by the specific caller [@hardy1988confused].

Extended autonomous execution also confronts the reality that multi-step external workflows cannot be rolled back atomically. Garcia-Molina and Salem developed sagas to manage long-running transactions, coordinating forward progress through predefined compensating actions when operations fail midway [@garciamolina1987sagas]. At interface boundaries, Meyer's design by contract established that modular software reliability depends on explicit, executable preconditions, postconditions, and invariants [@meyer1992applying]. Autonomous agents reopen each of these classical security and reliability challenges simultaneously. Because language models interleave data interpretation with control flow, external data cannot be assumed benign. @greshake2023not demonstrated that indirect prompt injection turns untrusted external content into instructions the model may follow. The result shows that for an agent guided by natural language, read access is itself an exposure, because what the agent reads can steer every action it proposes, even though only the runtime can grant those actions.

- **The Protection of Information in Computer Systems** [@saltzer1975]. The classic formulation of protection mechanisms for computer systems, including least privilege, complete mediation, and fail-safe defaults. This paper provides the conceptual foundation for modern tool authorization, sandboxing, and privilege boundaries in agent architectures.
- **End-to-End Arguments in System Design** [@saltzer1984endtoend]. The foundational rationale for placing validation checks at the application endpoints that maintain task semantics. In agent engineering, it clarifies why intermediate generation fluency cannot certify end-to-end task completion.
- **Basic Concepts and Taxonomy of Dependable and Secure Computing** [@avizienis2004basic]. The standard taxonomy distinguishing faults, errors, and failures across computing systems. It provides the disciplined vocabulary needed to diagnose agent failure modes, including the fail-plausible errors characteristic of foundation models.
- ***Principles of Computer System Design*** [@saltzer2009]. A comprehensive textbook on system decomposition, atomicity, virtualization, and protection. It supplies the essential systems foundation for building resilient agent orchestrators, runtimes, and tool harnesses.
- ***Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction*** [@sutton2018reinforcement]. The definitive treatise on sequential decision-making in dynamic environments. It provides the formal vocabulary of states, actions, rewards, and environment trajectories that underpins the execution model in this chapter.
- **ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models** [@yao2023react]. The seminal paper demonstrating that interleaving reasoning traces with tool invocations enables language models to solve multi-step problems. Reading it alongside this chapter highlights the boundary between the model's proposed actions and the external system responsible for executing and verifying them.

## Exercises {#sec-vol3-01_introduction-exercises}

All quantities below are hypothetical problem givens, chosen to be round, and describe no particular model, provider, or deployment. Unless a problem says otherwise, assume step errors are independent, each attempt costs the same in expectation, and "accepted" means accepted under a fixed task contract.

**1. How far can an unchecked repair run? (Basic).** A repair agent takes steps that are each correct with probability 0.98, and no step is checked before the next one builds on it.

(a) Using @eq-vol3-horizon-compounding, compute task success at horizons of 20 and 60 turns.
(b) Find the per-step error rate that would hold the 60-turn task at 80 percent success, and how many times lower it is than the current error rate. Confirm the answer with the small-$\PerStepErrorRate$ form $\PerStepErrorRate \TurnHorizon \approx -\ln(0.8)$.
(c) Instead of a better model, the runtime inserts a check after every 10 turns that detects any incorrect step in that segment and reruns the segment from the preceding checkpoint. Assuming the check is perfect and free, compute the expected number of turns to finish the 60-turn task, and compare it with rerunning the whole unchecked trajectory until it succeeds. State which lever to pull first and the property of the check on which the answer depends.

**2. A token discount or a better context? (Basic).** An attempt at a repair task spends \$1.80 on model tokens and \$1.20 on the sandbox, tests, and review, and 25 percent of attempts are accepted. The runtime retries until acceptance.

(a) Compute the expected number of attempts and the cost per accepted task from @eq-vol3-cost-per-accepted-task.
(b) A provider offers a 40 percent token discount; alternatively, a context change raises acceptance to 30 percent at the original attempt cost. Compute the cost per accepted task under each, and under both together.
(c) Find the acceptance probability that matches the discount. Explain why the comparison comes out differently from the chapter's notebook (\ref{nbk-01-cost-per-accepted}), naming the quantity that decides which lever wins.

**3. Placing a workload in H·S·A (Basic).** A log-triage agent runs about 15 turns per incident and spends \$0.50 on tokens per task. Consider three versions of its grant: (i) it reads logs and writes a summary to a scratch file; (ii) it also opens tickets in a shared tracker, and any ticket can be closed again; (iii) it also rolls back a production deployment, and a wrong rollback causes an outage costing \$2,000 that cannot be undone. In version (iii), 2 percent of rollbacks are wrong.

(a) Place each version on the state and authority axes of @fig-vol3-hsa-taxonomy, justifying each level by the consequence of the operation rather than its name.
(b) For version (iii), compute the expected loss per task from wrong rollbacks and express it as a multiple of the token cost.
(c) A human approval step costs \$5 per rollback and stops 90 percent of wrong ones. Compute the expected cost per task with approval, and state which exposure binds this workload.
(d) Specify all five task-contract fields for version (iii): the useful incident-triage goal and its negative scope, the deployment baseline and execution environment, the permitted actions and approval boundary, bounded diagnostic observations, and independent completion criteria. Name one limitation of the evidence that would require an unresolved outcome or further review.

**4. Paying for checks inside the horizon (Intermediate).** A repair task runs 50 turns with per-step error 0.02. Each turn costs \$0.04 in tokens, and each attempt pays \$1.00 to prepare a fresh sandbox. Under policy A, only a sealed test at the end checks the result; it accepts an attempt exactly when every step was correct, and a rejected attempt restarts from scratch. Under policy B, the same sandbox is kept and a check costing \$0.10 runs after every 10 turns, detecting any incorrect step in that segment, which is then rerun from the last checkpoint.

(a) Compute the acceptance probability and cost per accepted task under policy A.
(b) Compute the expected cost per accepted task under policy B, and the expected number of turns under each policy.
(c) Find the per-check cost at which policy B stops paying. Then critique the assumption that makes B look so strong: what happens to the calculation if the intermediate check is a visible test the agent can fit its patch to? Specify independent final evidence and concurrency coverage appropriate to this repair, using @sec-vol3-intro-invariant-closure, and explain why sealing a sequential test alone would not establish that the race condition is fixed.

**5. When the loss is not in the tokens (Intermediate; second lighthouse).** The remediation agent (lighthouse \ref{lhs-vol3-remediation-agent}) spends \$2 on tokens per attempt. Each attempt ends by proposing one configuration change that is correct with probability 0.95; a wrong change that commits costs \$20,000 in total. A human approval step costs \$15 of on-call time and delays restoration by 6 minutes, during which the ongoing incident costs \$50 per minute. Approval passes every correct change and rejects 90 percent of wrong ones; a rejected proposal starts a new attempt, which needs approval again.

(a) Without approval, every proposal commits. Compute the expected cost per task, including expected loss.
(b) With approval, compute the probability that an attempt ends in a commit, the expected attempts per task, the expected attempt spend, the probability the committed change is wrong, and the total expected cost per task.
(c) Find the incident cost per minute above which approval stops paying.
(d) For the repair agent, the chapter's levers were acceptance and horizon. Show numerically why halving the token price is irrelevant here, and name the binding constraint of this lighthouse and the H·S·A level that makes it bind.

**6. Workflow, loop, or both? (Intermediate).** A fixed workflow attempt for a support query costs \$0.60; a model-directed loop attempt costs \$1.80. Half the queries are routine, where the workflow is accepted with probability 0.55 and the loop with 0.80. The other half are novel, where the workflow is accepted with probability 0.05 and the loop with 0.70. Each query retries its chosen architecture until acceptance.

(a) Compute the cost per accepted task for each architecture on each query class, and the mean over the population if every query uses the workflow, and if every query uses the loop.
(b) A perfect router sends routine queries to the workflow and novel ones to the loop. Compute the mean cost per accepted query.
(c) A real router costs \$0.05 per query and sends a fraction $\MisroutedQueryFraction$ of each class to the wrong architecture. Compute the mean cost at $\MisroutedQueryFraction = 0.05$ and find the $\MisroutedQueryFraction$ at which routing stops beating the loop alone. What does this imply about where to spend engineering effort, and what must be held fixed for the comparison to be valid?

**7. Retries that repeat one mistake (Advanced).** Each attempt at a repair task costs \$2.00, and the retry budget allows 4 attempts. Of the tasks, 70 percent are easy, accepted with probability 0.70 per attempt; the rest are hard, and because each retry rereads the transcript and repeats the same mistaken hypothesis, a hard task is accepted with probability only 0.05 per attempt. Assume attempts are independent conditional on the task being easy or hard; the repeated hypothesis lowers the hard-task acceptance rate rather than making every retry share one outcome. Tasks not accepted within the budget end unresolved, and their spend stays in the numerator.

(a) An analyst pools the cohort into one mean acceptance probability and applies the independent-retry formulas. Compute the pooled acceptance, the predicted success within the budget, and the predicted cost per accepted task.
(b) Compute the actual acceptance within the budget, expected spend per task, and measured cost per accepted task under the mixture. By what factor did the pooled model understate the cost?
(c) Redesign the retry. Retries 2 through 4 start from a fresh context carrying only the failed test result, which costs \$2.50 per retry and raises a hard task's retry acceptance to 0.25 while leaving easy tasks unchanged. Compute the new acceptance within the budget and cost per accepted task, and argue whether the redesign should ship. What does the result say about treating $\AcceptanceProbability$ as a property of the model rather than of the whole attempt?

**8. Should the repair agent deploy its own patches? (Advanced).** A team produces 200 patches that pass the sealed tests each day. Of these patches, 3 percent are in fact wrong. A wrong patch that reaches production costs \$5,000. The team proposes letting the agent deploy directly. Two alternatives are on the table. A reviewer costing \$25 per patch catches 80 percent of the wrong patches that tests pass, and waiting for review delays each patch by 4 hours valued at \$10 per hour. Alternatively, a canary rollout costing \$5 per patch exposes a small slice of traffic and rolls back automatically, bounding the cost of a wrong patch to \$500.

(a) Place the direct-deploy proposal and the canary design on the H·S·A authority axis, and explain what changes the level.
(b) Compute the expected cost per patch and per day for direct deploy, review, and canary.
(c) Critique the canary design. Name one class of change for which automatic rollback is not an adequate reversal, state what authority level such a change returns to, and specify the contract change (permitted actions and completion criteria) that should route it back to review.

::: {.callout-chapter-connection title="From task responsibilities to the model call"}

Of the six phases every turn passes through, only the second belongs to the model, and each of the other five depends on knowing exactly what that phase delivers. When the repair agent asks to inspect the connection pool, the runtime may receive a complete tool request, a request cut off before it is whole, or no response at all, and each outcome requires different handling. @Sec-vol3-foundation-model follows that single inspection call from request to bill, establishing what one call reads, how its status reports completion, and what it costs. The single call sits at the origin of the H·S·A exposure space, so this invocation contract becomes the baseline from which every later part measures a departure.

:::
